title: Narcissism & Personality
description: Start with two introductory modules on the essential ideas and how to reason from evidence. Then practise applying the ideas in a detailed case.

glossary.definition: A tendency that appears with some consistency across situations. One behaviour is a clue, not a complete measure of a trait.
glossary.example: Someone regularly seeks recognition in different groups over many months.
glossary.limit: A single boast after good news is not a stable personality description.

glossary.definition: An attempt to protect oneself from information that feels threatening. It can appear in anyone, especially when something important feels at risk.
glossary.example: A worker argues sharply when asked to correct the credit on a presentation.
glossary.limit: Defensiveness does not reveal whether the criticism was fair or whether the person has a disorder.

glossary.definition: When feeling acceptable or valuable depends heavily on meeting a particular condition, such as appearing competent.
glossary.example: A small correction feels like proof of being a failure because reputation carries enormous weight.
glossary.limit: Wanting approval is common; the extent and cost of dependence matter.

glossary.definition: A clinical pattern considered through its persistence, pervasiveness and effects on functioning. It requires much more evidence than one argument.
glossary.example: A clinician investigates a long history across relationships before making any diagnostic judgement.
glossary.limit: A difficult interaction cannot establish a diagnosis, and a diagnosis cannot explain every action.

nodes.title: Start here
nodes.body:
People use ‘narcissist’ to describe behaviour they find hurtful. The word covers more than one idea, and using it carelessly can stop us asking what actually happened.

What can someone's response to criticism tell us, and what remains unknown?
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: What personality trait means
nodes.body:
A tendency that appears with some consistency across situations. One behaviour is a clue, not a complete measure of a trait.

For example: Someone regularly seeks recognition in different groups over many months.

One important limit: A single boast after good news is not a stable personality description.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: Find the first concept
nodes.prompt: Consider this example: Someone regularly seeks recognition in different groups over many months. Which concept is most directly demonstrated, without claiming anything beyond the example?
nodes.explanation: The example most directly supports personality trait. A tendency that appears with some consistency across situations. One behaviour is a clue, not a complete measure of a trait. A single boast after good news is not a stable personality description.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: What defensiveness means
nodes.body:
An attempt to protect oneself from information that feels threatening. It can appear in anyone, especially when something important feels at risk.

For example: A worker argues sharply when asked to correct the credit on a presentation.

One important limit: Defensiveness does not reveal whether the criticism was fair or whether the person has a disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: What contingent self-worth means
nodes.body:
When feeling acceptable or valuable depends heavily on meeting a particular condition, such as appearing competent.

For example: A small correction feels like proof of being a failure because reputation carries enormous weight.

One important limit: Wanting approval is common; the extent and cost of dependence matter.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: What personality disorder means
nodes.body:
A clinical pattern considered through its persistence, pervasiveness and effects on functioning. It requires much more evidence than one argument.

For example: A clinician investigates a long history across relationships before making any diagnostic judgement.

One important limit: A difficult interaction cannot establish a diagnosis, and a diagnosis cannot explain every action.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

lessons.teach: Read what is said before deciding why anyone said it.

nodes.title: A situation, not a diagnosis
nodes.body:
Maya built the statistical analysis. Leo led the project. The final slide credits only Leo.

You can describe an event accurately while remaining uncertain about why it happened.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: Listen before you interpret
nodes.prompt: Follow the four messages. Keep the difference between the words said and their possible meaning in mind.
nodes.explanation: The purpose is to connect the term to what can actually be observed.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.
nodes.scenario: Maya built the statistical analysis. Leo led the project. The final slide credits only Leo.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Could we change the slide? It says you developed the analysis, but that was my work.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I thought we'd agreed I was taking ownership of the results.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Of presenting them, yes. I still think the analysis should be credited accurately.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: You don't understand what's riding on this. They're considering me for a promotion.

checks.prompt: What is the most careful conclusion we can draw from the exchange so far?

options.label: We can describe what each speaker requested, while treating any account of their motives as provisional.
options.feedback: This keeps the distinction between what was said and why it may have been said. The latter requires more evidence.

options.label: We can take the last speaker’s explanation as the main cause, because it is the latest information.
options.feedback: Order of speaking does not determine evidential quality; the earlier words still matter.

options.label: We can give the two speakers’ interpretations equal weight, regardless of which one fits the details.
options.feedback: Plausible alternatives can receive different weights when the observed details support them differently.

options.label: We can infer that one speaker has a stable psychological trait if their response appears defensive.
options.feedback: A single interaction may reflect a situation rather than a trait that persists across settings.

options.label: We can stop analysing the situation because multiple explanations remain logically possible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a reason to test explanations, not to abandon reasoning.

checks.explanation: People can be sincere about their experience and still have incomplete explanations of why events happened. One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
checks.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.

nodes.title: A description or an assumption?
nodes.prompt: Does the sentence report something we can check, or interpret what it might mean?
nodes.explanation: The spoken words are evidence about what was said. A theory of why somebody said them is an interpretation that may need testing.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

items.label: “Could we change the slide? It says you developed the analysis, but that was my work.”
Leo treats correction as a possible loss of professional standing. His need to appear capable may be giving a routine attribution dispute unusually high emotional stakes.
“I thought we'd agreed I was taking ownership of the results.”
Leo may hold a sincere but mistaken belief that leading the project includes ownership of its technical work.

nodes.title: Why the distinction matters
nodes.body:
Leo may hold a sincere but mistaken belief that leading the project includes ownership of its technical work.

One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

lessons.title: Two explanations can sound reasonable
lessons.teach: Evidence should be able to change which explanation you prefer.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Start with competing accounts
nodes.body:
Leo treats correction as a possible loss of professional standing. His need to appear capable may be giving a routine attribution dispute unusually high emotional stakes.

Another possibility: Leo may hold a sincere but mistaken belief that leading the project includes ownership of its technical work.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: What should we find out?
nodes.prompt: Both interpretations are plausible. What would actually help choose between them?
nodes.explanation: Compare how Leo treats credit and correction over time, including when his own reputation is not at stake. The question is what would change our view, rather than what would merely confirm it.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

options.label: Ask the speakers how intense their feelings were and use the stronger reaction to identify the main cause.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling does not establish its cause.

options.label: Ask for a longer account from the speaker who was most upset, since they experienced the largest impact.
options.feedback: The account matters, but the amount of distress is not a direct test of someone else’s motive.

options.label: Compare how Leo treats credit and correction over time, including when his own reputation is not at stake.
options.feedback: This observation could make a meaningful difference between the competing explanations.

options.label: Find a second argument and see whether it sounds similar without comparing what changed.
options.feedback: A similar argument can occur for different reasons; comparison requires the relevant circumstances.

options.label: Ask an uninvolved friend to guess which personality type best describes the speaker.
options.feedback: A personality guess is less useful than identifying a testable difference between the proposed processes.

nodes.title: Something new has been found
nodes.body: A message from last month shows Leo thanking Maya for developing the analysis. Yesterday he told a director he had developed it personally.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: Revise your view
nodes.prompt: Which response to this new information is justified?
nodes.explanation: The messages weaken the role-confusion explanation and strengthen the possibility of knowing misattribution. Concern about reputation could still influence his response.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

options.label: Keep the original explanation because it initially fitted the facts.
options.feedback: A reasonable earlier account can be revised as new evidence appears.

options.label: Prefer the explanation that most closely matches the new detail, while keeping other plausible causes open.
options.feedback: This revises confidence in response to information rather than to the apparent sophistication of the theory.

options.label: Treat the new evidence as decisive proof of a single hidden intention.
options.feedback: The evidence can favour an account without establishing complete access to another person’s motives.

options.label: Give every explanation identical weight because certainty is impossible.
options.feedback: Uncertainty does not require all accounts to be equally likely.

options.label: Ignore the new detail until each speaker independently agrees on its meaning.
options.feedback: Agreement may help cooperation, but it is not a prerequisite for evaluating evidence.

lessons.title: Ready for a real case
lessons.teach: You have the concepts. Now practise using them without jumping beyond the evidence.
lessons.objective: Apply foundations to observable evidence, uncertainty and proportional decisions.

nodes.title: Watch the conversation
nodes.prompt: Read the exchange one message at a time, then work from what the characters actually said.
nodes.sources: Pincus et al. (2009), Pathological Narcissism Inventory; DSM-5-TR, personality functioning.
nodes.scenario: Maya developed the statistical analysis. Leo managed the project and the presentation credits the analysis to him.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The slide says you developed the analysis. I completed that part.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: I led the project. We agreed I would take ownership.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: Of presenting the results, yes. I still want my work acknowledged.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: You have no idea how much this promotion matters. They need to see me as capable.

turns.speaker: a
turns.text: The slide can show that you led the project and I developed the analysis.

turns.speaker: b
turns.text: If we change it now, they'll think I've been taking credit for something I couldn't do.

checks.prompt: Which psychological interpretation is currently best supported?

options.label: Leo believes project leadership ordinarily includes public credit for technical work.

lessons.title: Choose a workable response
lessons.teach: Choose a response that serves a practical aim even when the other person does not cooperate.

nodes.title: Your influence has limits
nodes.body:
One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.

An intervention can be reasonable even when the other person refuses it.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: Choose the next step
nodes.prompt: Your aim is to address the immediate concern while leaving room for a useful conversation.
nodes.explanation: The first response is a proportionate attempt to address the problem directly. Escalation may be legitimate if that attempt fails. One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.
nodes.scenario: Maya built the statistical analysis. Leo led the project. The final slide credits only Leo.

evidenceOptions.label: Leo may hold a sincere but mistaken belief that leading the project includes ownership of its technical work.
Leo treats correction as a possible loss of professional standing. His need to appear capable may be giving a routine attribution dispute unusually high emotional stakes.
A previous disagreement may have shaped the response, making the present conversation part of a longer pattern.
evidenceOptions.feedback: History could matter, but that earlier pattern has not yet been established.

evidenceOptions.label: Leo may be responding primarily to the timing of the correction, because changing a finished presentation could look like an admission of carelessness.
evidenceOptions.feedback: Timing could matter, but Leo explicitly connects the issue to how competent he appears.

responseOptions.label: If we can't correct the attribution together, I'll ask the project lead to review it before publication.
Your leadership deserves credit, and so does the analysis I completed. Can we put both roles on the slide before it goes out?
Ask each person to set out their own immediate concern before deciding whether to escalate.
responseOptions.feedback: This can reveal different priorities, but it may also delay an urgent factual correction.

nodes.title: If the first response fails
nodes.prompt: The other person rejects a reasonable direct request and the practical concern is unresolved. What next?
nodes.explanation: Escalation can be proportionate when a direct attempt has failed. Its safety and usefulness depend on the situation. One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

options.label: Repeat reassurance until the other person no longer experiences the issue as threatening.
options.feedback: Reassurance can help but cannot guarantee action on a concrete problem.

options.label: If we can't correct the attribution together, I'll ask the project lead to review it before publication.
options.feedback: This makes the unresolved issue reviewable without needing to diagnose the other person.

options.label: Leo may understand project ownership differently from Maya and interpret her request as a challenge to their agreed roles.
options.feedback: This can explain the initial dispute; his later emphasis on promotion suggests the stakes may extend beyond job descriptions.

options.label: What do you think a correction would lead the directors to conclude about your leadership?
options.feedback: A further question can clarify motives, but may delay resolution when the refusal is already clear.

nodes.title: What might change next?
nodes.prompt: The other person may disagree. Which response-and-outcome pairing best protects the practical concern without assuming cooperation?
nodes.explanation: A sound response is judged by what it makes possible, not by whether it can instantly change somebody else. Your leadership deserves credit, and so does the analysis I completed. Can we put both roles on the slide before it goes out?
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.

A concrete correction or next step is proposed. Agreement remains uncertain.
The immediate tension may ease without settling the underlying concern or establishing anyone’s motive.
outcomes.feedback: Short-term relief is possible, but the question asks what the proposed response would most directly change.

nodes.title: Correct the inference
nodes.prompt: Someone says: “That tells us what sort of person they really are.” Which revision is most defensible?
nodes.explanation: A working interpretation can be informative without being a diagnosis. One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.

options.label: Because an alternative is possible, every explanation should be treated as equally likely until we know the person well.
options.feedback: Possible explanations need not be equally supported. We should compare their fit with the actual evidence.

nodes.title: Which evidence matters most?
nodes.prompt: You want to distinguish the working hypothesis from its strongest alternative. Which investigation would provide the most discriminating information?
nodes.explanation: Investigate a difference that the rival explanations predict. Compare how Leo treats credit and correction over time, including when his own reputation is not at stake.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.

options.label: Ask both people to describe how strongly they felt during the conversation.
options.feedback: The strength of a feeling matters, but it does not establish its cause.

options.label: Compare how Leo treats credit and correction over time, including when his own reputation is not at stake.
options.feedback: This gathers information that could strengthen or weaken the explanation, rather than merely confirming an impression.

options.label: Ask the person affected whether the behaviour seems consistent with their overall impression of the speaker.
options.feedback: Impact and perception matter for responding; they are less decisive about the other person’s hidden motives.

options.label: Find one more occasion when the characters disagreed, without checking what the circumstances were.
options.feedback: Another incident is useful only if we compare the circumstances and plausible explanations.

options.label: Observe whether Leo accepts corrections that do not affect how his competence is presented to senior colleagues.
options.feedback: This comparison could distinguish a general objection to correction from a reputation-specific concern.

lessons.title: Try it in another situation
lessons.teach: Apply the way of reasoning to a different situation. Do not import the first case’s verdict.

nodes.title: A new situation
nodes.body:
At a family dinner, Daniel dismisses his sister's achievement each time relatives praise her, then accuses her of trying to embarrass him when she asks him to stop.

Decide what you can infer from this example without assuming the same explanation must apply.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

nodes.title: Apply the method elsewhere
nodes.prompt: Consider this different situation: At a family dinner, Daniel dismisses his sister's achievement each time relatives praise her, then accuses her of trying to embarrass him when she asks him to stop. What is the strongest next step?
nodes.explanation: Transfer the reasoning method rather than an explanation from the first case. One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.counterexample: One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.
nodes.sources: Pincus & Lukowitsky (2010), Pathological narcissism and narcissistic personality disorder; APA DSM-5-TR personality disorder framework.

options.label: Treat the visible similarity as a reliable indication that the behaviour has the same psychological function.
options.feedback: Similar behaviours can protect very different interests depending on the context.

options.label: Consider what the person could be trying to gain or avoid, then test that explanation against the circumstances and credible alternatives.
options.feedback: This asks what the behaviour might accomplish and how we could check.

options.label: Postpone all interpretation until the person can give an account of their private motives.
options.feedback: A perfect self-report may be unavailable. Tentative, revisable inferences can still be useful.

options.label: Judge whether the behaviour is socially acceptable first, since that provides the best evidence about why it happened.
options.feedback: Judging the consequences of a behaviour is important, but consequences do not by themselves establish motive.

nodes.title: An idea worth carrying forward
nodes.body:
Leo treats correction as a possible loss of professional standing. His need to appear capable may be giving a routine attribution dispute unusually high emotional stakes.

One defensive conversation cannot establish an enduring narcissistic pattern or a personality disorder.

The purpose of the exercise is to make a better-supported judgement and choose a proportionate next step.

glossary.definition: A tendency that appears with some consistency across situations. One behaviour is a clue, not a complete measure of a trait.
glossary.example: Someone regularly seeks recognition in different groups over many months.
glossary.limit: A single boast after good news is not a stable personality description.

glossary.definition: An attempt to protect oneself from information that feels threatening. It can appear in anyone, especially when something important feels at risk.
glossary.example: A worker argues sharply when asked to correct the credit on a presentation.
glossary.limit: Defensiveness does not reveal whether the criticism was fair or whether the person has a disorder.

glossary.definition: When feeling acceptable or valuable depends heavily on meeting a particular condition, such as appearing competent.
glossary.example: A small correction feels like proof of being a failure because reputation carries enormous weight.
glossary.limit: Wanting approval is common; the extent and cost of dependence matter.

glossary.definition: A clinical pattern considered through its persistence, pervasiveness and effects on functioning. It requires much more evidence than one argument.
glossary.example: A clinician investigates a long history across relationships before making any diagnostic judgement.
glossary.limit: A difficult interaction cannot establish a diagnosis, and a diagnosis cannot explain every action.
